target: AG1's claim that making Election Day a national holiday would directly remove scheduling barriers for voters who work or attend school.
objection: A federal holiday does not reliably remove those barriers because private employers are generally not required to give paid time off, so many retail, restaurant, caregiving, delivery, and other service workers would still be scheduled to work or would have to use unpaid time. The holiday therefore does not consistently solve the actual time-conflict problem faced by low-income workers.

target: AG1's idea that a holiday will make voting a more important civic celebration and thereby strengthen participation.
objection: This is not a substantive rebuttal made in the transcript; no direct objection to the civic-celebration argument appears beyond the turnout-effectiveness and access critiques. (Omitted per transcript constraints.)

target: AG2's claim that a federal holiday will not reliably change the schedule enough to matter.
objection: A federal holiday can still reduce scheduling conflicts because it shifts community-wide norms: schools close, many workplaces operate on reduced holiday hours, and voters can use a common daytime window even if some private employers remain open. The holiday changes the default schedule enough to help many people.

target: AG1's assumption that a holiday will change employers' and workers' incentives enough to reduce scheduling conflicts.
objection: Without a mandate, a holiday does not reliably change private employers' incentives or schedules; many workplaces simply keep operating, so workers still face the same choice between voting and working. The calendar signal therefore does not guarantee reduced conflict.

target: AG2's claim that a federal holiday will not create a common daytime opportunity for voting.
objection: A holiday does create a broader daytime opportunity because communities run on holiday schedules, schools are closed, and many employers reduce operations. The point is not that every employer closes, but that the overall schedule shifts enough to make voting easier for many people.

target: AG1's assumption that the holiday will translate into a common daytime opportunity for low-income workers.
objection: Federal holiday status does not compel private employers to close or provide paid time off, so many shift-based workplaces still operate and workers may still have to choose between work and voting. The calendar change is mostly symbolic for those workers unless employers must actually grant time off.

target: AG2's assumption that without employer mandates a holiday cannot create meaningful daytime access.
objection: The mechanism is broader than mandatory paid leave: school closures, altered household routines, and reduced holiday staffing across many employers create a shared daytime window. International practice in countries that hold elections on holidays or weekends also supports the idea that calendar timing can improve access.

target: AG1's claim that a holiday creates a common daytime voting window and reduces scheduling conflicts.
objection: In many retail, food service, caregiving, logistics, and similar jobs, federal holidays do not mean closure or reduced staffing, so low-income workers still face the same time conflict. A civic holiday changes symbolism more than scheduling reality unless employers are required to grant voting time.

target: AG2's argument that a national holiday is not a reliable turnout reform and would disadvantage low-income workers.
objection: The central problem is weekday scheduling, especially work and school conflicts. A federal holiday changes those baseline conditions by closing schools and shifting many workplaces to reduced holiday operations, creating a broader daytime opportunity for voting and helping the workers most harmed by tight schedules.

target: AG1's reliance on OECD countries and public support as evidence that a holiday would reduce scheduling barriers in the U.S.
objection: Those facts do not prove the causal mechanism. OECD countries differ in polling hours, voting channels, and labor norms, so their holiday elections do not show that a U.S. federal holiday alone would create meaningful time to vote. Public support shows acceptability, not effectiveness.

target: AG1's assumption that federal holiday status will produce broadly usable daytime opportunities for low-income workers.
objection: Federal holiday status does not require private employers to close or provide time off, especially in sectors like retail, restaurants, caregiving, and delivery. Therefore the holiday may leave the actual scheduling constraint unchanged for the workers who most need relief.

target: AG2's claim that low-income workers still would not get meaningful daytime access because some employers remain open.
objection: The real barrier is not only paid leave; it is the community-level fit between voting tasks and normal weekday schedules. A holiday closes schools and shifts many employers to reduced operations, so even if some workplaces remain open, the overall number of scheduling collisions falls and voting becomes easier for many people.

target: AG1's assumption that a federal holiday will produce a predictable daytime window for low-income workers.
objection: That assumption depends on employers shifting staffing enough to give workers daytime access, but federal holiday status does not require private employers to close or provide paid or unpaid time. So the holiday does not guarantee the usable time window the argument needs.

target: AG2's use of OECD comparisons and public support to dismiss the holiday mechanism.
objection: The relevant question is whether moving elections away from ordinary weekday schedules helps with access, and the international practice is consistent with that mechanism. Even if it does not perfectly isolate every variable, it supports the idea that holiday timing can reduce scheduling barriers, and the strong bipartisan support shows the problem is widely recognized.
